confirmed.title: Tester function and control blocks break the closing-brace rule
confirmed.detail: 03-cpp.md applies to "**/*.cpp" and says: "Closing braces: a multi-line block ends on the line of its last statement, `return res;}`. This applies to control blocks, function bodies and lambda bodies, and nests: `}}`." In the tester, every multi-line function body and control block ends with `}` on a line of its own. Examples: fail (line 10), require (lines 13-16: the if block and the function body), pass (line 20), testAliases (line 37), testMacrosAndConstants (line 54), the random-history for loop and testIndexedSet (lines 101-102), testChminChmax (line 150), main (line 158), and the static_assert lambda (line 121). The header itself follows the rule; this is limited to the tester. Fix: move each closing brace onto its last statement's line, for example `std::abort();}` and `fail(expr, line);}}`. Behavior does not change.

confirmed.title: Packed-bool proxies print as 1/0 instead of true/false (slices of vector<bool>, views over non-const vector<bool>, bitset::reference)
confirmed.detail: The bool branch only matches T == bool exactly. A non-const vector<bool> range gives elements of type std::vector<bool>::reference (std::_Bit_reference). That type is not bool or arithmetic, and it is not a range, tuple or aggregate, so it reaches the ostream branch at line 99. That branch streams the implicit bool conversion without boolalpha. The plain vector prints {true, false}, but a borrowed slice or view of the same vector prints {1, 0}. This breaks the documented contract in 21-c01-verification.md that bool spells true/false. Contests often slice a visited/used grid (vector<vector<bool>>) with Debug::slice, so the case comes up in practice. The tester covers only const iteration of vector<bool> (line 367), where const_reference is plain bool. Confirmed with GCC 16.2: the vector prints {true, false}, but Debug::slice(v, 0, 1), std::views::all(v) and a vector<vector<bool>> slice print {1, 0} and {{1, 0}}. Fix: add a branch before the stream fallback, e.g. `else if constexpr (std::is_same_v<T, vector<bool>::reference> || requires { typename T::reference; } && ...)`. The simplest form is `else if constexpr (std::is_same_v<T, vector<bool>::reference>) { res += bool(x) ? "true" : "false"; }`. Optionally also handle the bitset<N>::reference proxy. Add tests for slice(v, ...) and views::all(v) over a non-const vector<bool>.

confirmed.title: Per-word assertion inside the fused-shift kernel's inner loop
confirmed.detail: In shiftedWord, `assert(i < a.size() && s < 64);` runs once per word. combineShift calls shiftedWord on every word of its scalar loop (lines 227 and 230), and that scalar path is the default on Codeforces, which runs with assertions on and no AVX2. 03-cpp.md says: "An assertion must not change an operation's asymptotic cost and must stay out of hot inner loops; check preconditions once at the entry of an operation." combineShift already establishes both facts at its entry: k < n gives d < a.size(), and s = k % 64. Measured impact is nil. At -O2 on a 65,536-bit set with 200,000 self-aliased Xor fused shifts, timings with the assert (0.23-0.25 s), without it, and with -DNDEBUG were all within noise, because GCC removes the check. So this breaks the rule as written but does not slow anything down. toString (line 265, through test()) and the string constructor (line 34, through set()) also assert once per bit, but they stay O(n). Fix: delete the assert at line 190, or move it into combineShift's entry as a single `assert(d < a.size())`.

confirmed.title: Bulk fixed-multiplier tests use only multiplier(MAX), which reduces to 0 or 1 for most tested moduli, so the AVX2 Shoup kernel is barely exercised
confirmed.detail: batches() builds exactly one fixed multiplier per modulus: `auto fixed = red.multiplier(MAX);`. Because 2^32-1 = 3*5*17*257*65537, value = MAX % m is 0 for m in {3, 5, 17, 65537, 2^32-1} and 1 for m in {2^31-1, 2^32-2}. 2^31 and the moduli 1 and 2 take the mask path. So the non-mask AVX2 Shoup kernel (03-barrett.hpp lines 80-89) only gets a factor that is neither 0 nor 1 for three moduli: 998244353, 1e9+7 and 2^31+1 (value 2^31-2). It is never tested with value = m-1, and never with a modulus near 2^32 combined with a nontrivial factor. That case pushes the residual close to 2^33 through the signed _mm256_cmpgt_epi64 correction. The 64-bit bulk Shoup has the same issue (2^64-1 also has the factors 3, 5, 17 and 65537), but it is a plain scalar loop, so that matters less. The scalar Multiplier::mul is well covered, but the 23-reduction.md feature map claims the bulk fixed products are covered as if the vector kernel had independent coverage. I found no wrong output: a differential run of 940,000 cases agreed with native %, including b=m-1, a in {2^32-1, m-1, random}, n=37, moduli 2^32-1, 2^32-5, 3221225473, 2^31+1 and random moduli, under -mavx2 and -mno-avx2 with ASan/UBSan. Fix: in batches(), also build multipliers for b = m-1 and for a random b, and check fixed.mul(ptr) against Wide(a)*b%m for each.

confirmed.title: Per-element assertions inside the bulk SIMD and scalar loops violate the hot-loop assertion rule and cost about 49% of AVX2 bulk throughput on judges that keep assertions
confirmed.detail: 00-Guidelines/03-cpp.md line 16 says: "Judges run with assertions enabled. An assertion must not change an operation's asymptotic cost and must stay out of hot inner loops; check preconditions once at the entry of an operation." The bulk kernels break this rule. The AVX2 loops of mul (line 94), mulLazy (line 106) and get (line 129) run an 8-iteration scalar loop of assert(a[i + j] < mod && b[i + j] < mod) on every vector step. The scalar tails and the whole 64-bit bulk path (lines 99, 111, 136) call the checked scalar mul/mulLazy/get, which assert again for each element, and red/redLazy assert a third time. The sibling 03-barrett.hpp checks only once at entry (assert(n >= 0 && ...)). The evidence in 23-reduction.md (rows at lines 101 and 108, the AVX2/scalar ratio of 0.40 and the eight-element threshold) was measured only with -O3 -DNDEBUG (03-reduction_benchmark.py line 50). Codeforces, the target judge, does not define NDEBUG, so those numbers do not describe the judge configuration. Suggested fix: remove the per-lane asserts from the AVX2 loops. Have the scalar tails and the 64-bit bulk loops call an unchecked reduction directly (for example out[i] = red(Wide(a[i]) * b[i]) without the operand asserts), or OR together a vector out-of-range mask and assert once after the loop. Then re-measure the benchmark without NDEBUG. Most of the existing bulk death tests (bulk-mul-a, bulk-get-a, bulk-lazy-a, ...) still pass if the check becomes a single post-loop or entry check.

confirmed.title: Optimality (outside the requested categories, so labelled style): constructing from int or lng always uses a software 128-bit division (__modti3)
confirmed.detail: This is the only finding that affects behavior; it is about speed, not correctness. The schema has no performance category, so it is filed as style. `norm` sends every signed integer through `lll r = lll(a) % lll(mod());`, whatever its width. GCC turns this into a call to `__modti3` at -O2, even when the modulus is a compile-time constant. That call runs on every `mint(i)`, every `x * 2` or `x + k` with an int operand, every int assignment and every `Value r = 1` inside pow. The Core full profile requires 'Extreme optimization' (01-principles.md), and the benchmark record in 24-modint.md never measures construction from native integers. confirmed.title: (Low) A moved-from Fenwick keeps its old n while v is empty, so in-contract calls index past the end of v
confirmed.detail: The implicit move constructor moves `v` (which becomes empty) but copies `int n`. The invariant `n == v.size()` breaks. Every entry assertion checks only against `n`, so after `auto b = std::move(a)` a call such as `a.add(0, 1)` or `a.prefixSum(a.n)` passes its precondition and then indexes an empty vector. That is undefined behavior; the build used here caught it only because the template enables libstdc++ assertions. The tester (line 98) only reassigns the moved-from object, so the gap is not exercised. Using a moved-from object is unusual in contest code, which is why this is low severity. DSU and other structures may share the pattern. Fix: either document that a moved-from Fenwick may only be assigned or destroyed, or drop the redundant `n` field and use `int(v.size())`. Dropping it would also remove the risk of public-state drift.

confirmed.title: get() and allQuery() return a dangling reference when T = bool (vector<bool> proxy)
confirmed.detail: `const T &get(int p) const { ... return tree[base + p]; }` (line 28) and `const T &allQuery() const { return tree[1]; }` (line 29) assume that `vector<T>::operator[] const` returns `const T&`. For T = bool, `vector<bool>::const_reference` is a plain `bool` prvalue, so both functions return a reference to a temporary. That is undefined behavior. The header contract allows any T with an associative f and an identity, and an OR/AND/XOR segment tree over bool is a common case. GCC 16.2 gives `-Wreturn-local-addr` for both lines. At -O2 the program crashes with a segfault. Under -fsanitize=address,undefined it reports 'reference binding to null pointer of type const bool' at 03-segmenttree.hpp:28:78 and 29:46, then a SEGV. The documented promise 'Returned references remain owned by this tree' is false for this T. Fix: declare both return types as `typename vector<T>::const_reference`, which is `const T&` for every T except bool and `bool` for bool. Otherwise add `static_assert(!std::is_same_v<T, bool>)` and document that restriction. Then add a bool payload case to the tester.

For `SqrtDecomp<lng> d({5})`, binding `{5}` to the int parameter is an identity conversion, while building a vector<T> needs a user-defined conversion. The int overload wins, so the result has 5 identity elements instead of one element 5. `SqrtRangeSum<lng> r({5})` does the same. This mismatches the usual container intuition (`vector<lng> v({5})` is [5]) and silently gives wrong sums for a singleton literal. Separately, SqrtDecomp's constructors (lines 18 and 21) are not `explicit`, so `void f(const SqrtDecomp<lng>&); f(7);` compiles and builds a 7-element structure. SqrtRangeSum and the sibling DSU mark their constructors explicit.
confirmed.repro: /tmp/sq_b.cpp: `SqrtDecomp<lng> d({5}); SqrtRangeSum<lng> r({5}); cout << d.n << ' ' << d.query(0,d.n) << ' ' << r.n << ' ' << r.sum(0,r.n);` prints `5 0 5 0` (expected n=1, sum 5). `f(7)` with `f(const SqrtDecomp<lng>&)` compiles and prints 7. Fix: mark both SqrtDecomp constructors explicit. Either add an `std::initializer_list<T>` overload or document that the vector form must be spelled `vector<T>{...}`.

confirmed.title: Constructor parameters are named `ID` and `f_`, outside the naming vocabulary
confirmed.detail: 03-cpp.md says: "fields and locals short lowercase or `snake_case`". The only uppercase exceptions are template parameters and "constructor size parameters such as `N` and `M`". `ID` is an identity value, not a size, so the exception does not cover it. The sibling SegmentTree (03-segmenttree.hpp line 19) uses `T id, F f` for the same concept, and the rule is "Use the same name for the same concept everywhere".
confirmed.repro: Lines 18 and 21: `T ID = T{}, F f_ = F{}) : id(std::move(ID)), f(std::move(f_))`. Fix: rename to `T id = T{}, F f = F{}) : id(std::move(id)), f(std::move(f))`, matching SegmentTree.

confirmed.title: Per-element precondition asserts sit inside the hot scan loops
confirmed.detail: 03-cpp.md says: "Judges run with assertions enabled. An assertion must not change an operation's asymptotic cost and must stay out of hot inner loops; check preconditions once at the entry of an operation." Line 76 has `assert(h >= 0)` inside monotone_detail::histogram's main loop. When matrixRectangle calls histogram, that assert runs n*m times even though the heights there are nonnegative by construction. Line 122 has `assert(x == 0 || x == 1)` inside the `matches` predicate, which runs once per cell in the row update loop on line 93. Severity is low: a benchmark of a 4000x4000 matrix and a 2e7-bar histogram showed no measurable gap between the assert and -DNDEBUG builds. The fix: check nonnegativity once at the entry of largestHistogramRectangle (e.g. `assert(std::ranges::all_of(a, [](lng x) { return x >= 0; }))`) and drop the assert from histogram. For largestBinaryRectangle, validate each row once before its update loop (or in a single pass at entry) instead of inside the per-cell predicate. The negative-height, late-negative-height, binary-negative-cell and binary-large-cell probes will still fire.

confirmed.title: Unary minus and perp narrow implicitly in list-initialization for int8_t/int16_t coordinates
confirmed.detail: The static_assert accepts any signed integral T, including int8_t and int16_t. For those types `-x` promotes to int. So `return {-x, -y};` (line 25), `return {-x, -y, -z};` (line 49) and perp's `return {-a.y, a.x};` (line 70) need a narrowing conversion inside list-initialization, which is ill-formed under [dcl.init.list]. confirmed.title: circleLineIntersectionApprox misclassifies exact integer tangencies along non-axis directions
confirmed.detail: The function normalises the direction first (u = (b - a) / |b - a|, which rounds each component), then takes z = dot(a - c.c, perp(u)) and tests d == c.r exactly. That stacks several roundings, so an exactly tangent line given by integer input often lands on the wrong side of r and returns 0 or 2 points instead of 1. I scanned r in 1..50, a in [-60,60]^2 and directions (3,4), (4,3), (-3,4), (5,12), (12,5), (8,15): 2244 of the 9818 exact tangencies were misclassified. The header disclaims certified topology near degeneracy, but here the error comes from operation order and costs nothing to avoid. Computing z = cross(b - a, a - c.c) / length(b - a) has one rounding (cross is exact for integer-valued long doubles, and hypot is exact for Pythagorean lengths), and it gets all 9818 cases right. Fix: let w = b - a and L = length(w); set z = cross(w, a - c.c) / L (the sign must match perp), keep the foot p = c.c + perp(w) * (z / L), and build u = w / L only for the half-chord offset.

Probe program: /tmp/circrev/a.cpp and /tmp/circrev/b.cpp.

confirmed.title: The small-angle switch in angleMinusSin at .01 is too low: up to 2e-15 relative error just above it

confirmed.title: Full-mode tester fails for seed 1: the Decimal Heron oracle misclassifies exactly degenerate dyadic sides
confirmed.detail: This is a tester defect, not a header defect. `heron()` sets `ctx.prec = 160` and then decides `valid = max(a, b, c) <= s` using rounded Decimal sides. The random fixtures (lines 86-92) scale integer sides by 2^k with |k| up to 7000, so each exact value has thousands of decimal digits. In the line-89 branch `c = rng.randint(0, a + b + 2)`, c can equal a+b, which gives an exactly degenerate triangle. Rounding to 160 digits breaks that equality and the oracle writes `valid=0, area=-1`. Seed 1, full mode, produces the sides 1.25, 7.125 and 5.875 times 2^-4096 (strtold gives 0xap-4099, 0xe.4p-4097, 0xb.cp-4097). Since 1.25 + 5.875 = 7.125 exactly, `heronAreaApprox` correctly returns true with area 0, and the tester then reports FAIL 'Heron triangle inequality classification'. The failure message prints the default placeholder strings expected=true actual=false, which are the reverse of the real values (oracle false, library true). The recorded seed 20260927 and quick seeds 1-5 pass, so the evidence run did not reach this case. Each full run has about 300 such random cases and the chance of c == a+b is roughly 1/1000 per case, so many seeds will fail. Fix: classify with exact arithmetic (`fa, fb, fc = map(Fraction, sides); valid = 2 * max(fa, fb, fc) <= fa + fb + fc`), compute the four Heron factors exactly as Fractions, and convert to Decimal only for the square root. Alternatively use a precision large enough for the exact dyadic expansions, as lines 82-85 already do with 11000 digits. Also pass the real booleans to `require` at tester.cpp line 78 so the reproducer is not misleading.

confirmed.title: excircle computes the semiperimeter gap x+y-z with avoidable cancellation: large error, or an assert, on well-conditioned thin triangles
confirmed.detail: `d = min(x, y) - (z - max(x, y))` subtracts nearly equal lengths when the angle at the opposite vertex is close to pi. The exradius and excenter here are well-conditioned in the coordinates: moving a coordinate by one ulp changes the gap only at second order. The loss comes from the formula. For TriangleApprox({0,0},{2,0},{1,h}).excircle(2, c), the reference is r = h/(sqrt(1+h^2)-1), which is 2e6 for h=1e-6 and 2e9 for h=1e-9 (checked with an 80-digit Decimal). The header returns relative errors of 4.0e-9 (h=1e-6), 3.7e-4 (h=1e-8) and 7.8e-2 (h=1e-9, r=1.8447e9 instead of 2e9). At h=1e-10, hypot rounds x and y to exactly 1, d becomes 0 and `assert(d > 0)` aborts, although the exradius 2e10 is representable. The contract does call 'rounded-zero gap' a precondition, but that wording hides an avoidable instability. Evidence lines 60 and 72 put the cancellation only in the tester's reference ('no implementation change'). In fact the implementation has the same cancellation, and the widened tolerance 64*eps*r*perimeter at tester.cpp:209 hides it. The equal-line-distance witness (tester.cpp:203) also cannot detect a wrong d, because the center error moves along the bisector. Fix: when dot(u,v) < 0, use the identity x+y-z = 2*cross(u,v)^2/((x*y - dot(u,v))*(x+y+z)); otherwise keep x+y-z. With this change the relative error is 0 to 2e-19 for h from 1e-3 to 1e-15 (tested in /tmp/trirev/fix.cpp). Then tighten the tester's exradius tolerance and add a thin obtuse excircle regression against a high-precision reference.

confirmed.title: GraphEdge and GraphArc have no complexity comment; method comments lack T:/M: labels
confirmed.detail: 03-cpp.md, Complexity comments: "One comment line directly above every struct and free function except template and debug code: `// T: O(...), M: O(...)`". `struct GraphEdge` (line 5) has no comment above it. `struct GraphArc` (line 6) has only the GraphEdge declaration above it. Sibling headers follow the rule for plain aggregates, for example 02-traversal.hpp:9 `// T: O(1), M: O(n) ...` above CycleWitness. Also, the method bounds at lines 35, 40 and 74 are written as bare `// O(n + m)` without the T:/M: components, even though the struct comments use S/U/Q/M and give no T. Fix: add `// T: O(1), M: O(1)` above each of the two aggregates, and rewrite the method comments as `// T: O(n + m), M: O(n + m) ...`.

confirmed.title: BFS tie-order contract (`Ties follow source/arc order`) has no oracle; a mutation that reverses adjacency order passes full mode
confirmed.detail: 02-traversal.hpp:51 documents that BFS ties follow source and arc order, which fixes `order`, `parent`, `parent_arc` and multi-source `root`. For BFS the tester checks only reachability, Floyd depth, that the parent arc is valid with depth+1, that the root is some source, and that layers are nondecreasing (lines 41-52). It never compares against an independent queue-order oracle, the way it does for DFS with the recursive oracle at lines 55-64. So the documented BFS tie behavior has no test, and the evidence's feature-to-test map claims more than is checked. Fix: add a plain FIFO BFS reference to `traversal()` for the `breadth` case. It should seed sources in order, skip duplicates and scan `g[u]` in order. Then compare `order`, `parent`, `parent_arc` and `root` exactly.

confirmed.title: Iterative DFS calls the asserting `g[u]` accessor twice per arc step in its innermost loop
confirmed.detail: 03-cpp.md says: "An assertion must not change an operation's asymptotic cost and must stay out of hot inner loops; check preconditions once at the entry of an operation." In `dfs`, every iteration of the frame loop evaluates `g[u].size()` (line 88) and `g[u][pos[u]++]` (line 90). `Graph::operator[]` and `CsrGraph::operator[]` (01-graph.hpp:23-24, 71-73) each run `assert(0 <= u && u < n)`, and CsrGraph also builds a span each time. That is two range asserts per arc step, under the judges' assert-enabled builds. The cost is constant-factor only, so this is low severity. bfs, connectedComponents and bipartiteCheck call `g[u]` once per vertex and are fine. Fix: look up the adjacency once per frame step, e.g. `const auto &adj = g[u];` (or `auto adj = g[u];` for span), and use `adj.size()` and `adj[pos[u]++]`. Or keep a per-frame adjacency handle on the explicit stack.
confirmed.repro: Rule quote above. Code: lines 88 and 90 of 04-Graphs/02-traversal.hpp, each `g[u]` going through 01-graph.hpp:24 `assert(0 <= u && u < n)`.

votes.reason: The finding holds. In 04-Graphs/02-traversal.hpp, the dfs frame loop runs once per arc step plus once per pop. Each time, it evaluates `g[u].size()` (line 88). When the vertex still has arcs, it also evaluates `g[u][pos[u]++]` (line 90). Graph::operator[] (01-graph.hpp:23-24) and CsrGraph::operator[] (01-graph.hpp:71-73) both run `assert(0 <= u && u < n)`, and CsrGraph also builds a subspan on every call. So each arc step runs two range asserts in the hottest loop of the function. 03-cpp.md:16 says assertions "must stay out of hot inner loops; check preconditions once at the entry of an operation". The compiler is not guaranteed to merge the two checks, because the write `pos[u]++` goes through an int* that may alias `g.n`. bfs, connectedComponents and bipartiteCheck fetch the adjacency once per vertex, so only dfs is affected. The cost is constant-factor only, so low severity as a style issue is accurate. I compiled and ran nothing, because the finding is about cost and code style rather than wrong output, and the code reading settles it.

I could not refute this finding; it holds. In /home/Ausp3x/Documents/CompProg Library/04-Graphs/02-traversal.hpp, `dfs` does two things on every pass of its `while (!path.empty())` loop. Line 88 evaluates `g[u].size()` and line 90 evaluates `g[u][pos[u]++]`. Every arc is handled by one pass of that loop, so each arc step calls the accessor twice. Graph::operator[] in /home/Ausp3x/Documents/CompProg Library/04-Graphs/01-graph.hpp asserts `0 <= u && u < n`. CsrGraph::operator[] runs the same assert and also builds a span with subspan. Section 03-cpp.md:16 says: "Judges run with assertions enabled. An assertion must not change an operation's asymptotic cost and must stay out of hot inner loops; check preconditions once at the entry of an operation." These asserts sit in the hottest loop of the algorithm. Their check is also redundant, because `u` always comes from `path`, which holds only vertices already in range. So this breaks the rule as written. The cost is constant-factor only and the result is never wrong, which is why low-severity style is the right rating. The fix is correct: take one adjacency handle per step and use it for both the size check and the element read. I did not compile anything, since this is a style claim and needs no runtime repro.

I could not refute this finding. It is accurate. In 04-Graphs/02-traversal.hpp, `dfs` evaluates `g[u].size()` on line 88 and `g[u][pos[u]++]` on line 90 on every pass of the path loop, which runs once per arc. Both overloads of `operator[]` run `assert(0 <= u && u < n)` on every call: `Graph` at 01-graph.hpp:23-24 and `CsrGraph` at 01-graph.hpp:71-73. `CsrGraph` also rebuilds a span through `subspan` on every call. So each arc step runs two range asserts that judges compile in. That conflicts with 03-cpp.md line 16: assertions "must stay out of hot inner loops; check preconditions once at the entry of an operation." `u` always comes from `path`, and every vertex on `path` has already been checked, either as a source asserted at entry or as a stored arc's `to`. So these asserts are redundant inside the loop. Hoisting the lookup once per frame step (`const auto &adj = g[u];` or `auto adj = g[u];`) removes the duplicate check without changing behaviour. The finding correctly calls this a constant-factor style issue, not a correctness bug, so I did not need to compile a repro.

confirmed.title: Multi-line block closed as '; }}}' instead of ';}}}' (closing-brace rule)
confirmed.detail: The `if (i == g.n - 1 && !out.negative[e.to]) {` block opens on line 163 and spans two lines, but line 164 ends `ready.push_back(e.to); }}}` with a space before the brace that closes it. Line 212 has the same problem: the `if (out.reachable[u]) {` block from line 211 ends `is_proc[u] = true; }}}`. 03-cpp.md says: "Closing braces: a multi-line block ends on the line of its last statement, `return res;}`." The spaced form `{ x; }` is only for single-line blocks. These are the only two places in the header that break the rule. The other 16 multi-line closings use `;}`. Fix: line 164 should end `ready.push_back(e.to);}}}` and line 212 should end `is_proc[u] = true;}}}`.

confirmed.title: Eight public free-function overloads, including all of dagLongestPaths, have no complexity comment
confirmed.detail: 03-cpp.md says: "One comment line directly above every struct and free function except template and debug code: `// T: O(...), M: O(...)`". These overloads have no comment above them at all: bfsShortestPaths(g,int) at line 67, zeroOneBfs(g,int) at 87, dijkstra(g,int) at 105, dijkstraDense(DenseGraph,int) at 124, dagShortestPaths(g,int,bool) at 143, both dagLongestPaths overloads at 146 and 148, and bellmanFord(g,int) at 182. dagLongestPaths is a separately named inventory operation, so it is entirely undocumented. The sibling verified header 04-Graphs/02-traversal.hpp does comment its single-source overloads (lines 69 and 100: `// T: O(n + m), M: O(n), including output; s must be in [0,n).`), so this header breaks the established convention. Fix: add a `// T: ..., M: ...` line above each overload. For example, put `// T: O(n + m), M: O(n), including output. Maximum-weight paths; directed only, signed weights.` above dagLongestPaths, and single-source bounds without the k term above the int overloads.

confirmed.title: relax() runs two assertions on every relaxation inside the hot loops of all algorithms
confirmed.detail: ShortestPathResult::relax checks endpoint ranges (line 39) and `reachable[e.from] && a >= 0` (line 40) on every call. bellmanFord (line 161), dijkstra (103), zeroOneBfs (83), dijkstraDense (122) and dagShortestPaths (141) all call relax inside their per-arc inner loops. In bellmanFord that is O(n*m) assertion evaluations, and bellmanFord already tests `out.reachable[e.from]` itself just before the call. 03-cpp.md says: "Judges run with assertions enabled. An assertion ... must stay out of hot inner loops; check preconditions once at the entry of an operation." Measured on the Bellman-Ford fixture below, the build with assertions ran about 5-10% slower than -DNDEBUG (0.165/0.174 s vs 0.150/0.148 s). The difference is noisy and does not change asymptotics, but it is exactly the placement the rule forbids. Fix: move the arc-validity checks into an unchecked internal relaxation step used by the algorithms (they already validate sources and arcs at entry), and keep the asserting public relax() only for external callers.

confirmed.title: Inventory operations kruskal/primSparse/primDense/boruvka (maximum) are absent
confirmed.detail: The P010 inventory row lists `kruskal (maximum); primSparse (maximum); primDense (maximum); boruvka (maximum)`. None of the four engines takes a maximum flag. kruskal(const G&), primSparse(const G&), primDense(const DenseGraph&) and boruvka(const G&) only build minimum forests, so these operations are absent. The row is already `partial` and names them under `missing:`, so this is a tracked gap rather than a mislabelled status. It still blocks marking the package verified. Most of the plumbing exists: mst_detail::edgeLess/edgeOrder already take `bool maximum` (lines 14, 19), and KruskalReconstruction uses it. One caveat for primDense: DenseGraph::best (01-graph.hpp) keeps only the minimum-weight parallel arc. A maximum dense Prim therefore needs its own max-edge view or has to scan the multigraph; it cannot simply flip the comparator.
confirmed.repro: Add `Graph g(2); g.addEdge(0,1,1); g.addEdge(0,1,5);` and call `kruskal(g, true)`. It does not compile because there is no overload with a maximum flag. Fix: add `bool maximum = false` to kruskal/primSparse/boruvka and pass it to edgeOrder/edgeLess. For primSparse the set key also has to be negated or reordered for maximum. Add a maximum dense view for primDense. Then extend verify() in 06-mst_tester.cpp to check each against oracle.maximum through forest(g, result, oracle, true).

confirmed.title: Precondition assert runs inside the sort comparator and per-element loops through Interval::bounds
confirmed.detail: Interval::bounds (line 16) runs assert(l <= r) on every call. finishOrder's sort comparator (line 37) calls bounds twice per comparison, so the assert runs O(n * log(n)) times inside sort's inner loop, and the bounds arithmetic is redone each time. Per-element loops also call bounds again after finishOrder already checked every interval: line 124 (minimumIntervalStabbing), line 137 (maximumIntervalSchedule), and lines 150 and 155 (weightedIntervalSchedule calls bounds twice per item). 03-cpp.md says: "An assertion must not change an operation's asymptotic cost and must stay out of hot inner loops; check preconditions once at the entry of an operation." The asymptotic cost is unchanged, so only the hot-loop part of the rule is broken. Fix: in finishOrder, compute bounds once per interval into a vector<pair<lll,lll>> (asserting there) and sort and return ids keyed on that cached vector. Callers then reuse the cached bounds instead of calling a[i].bounds(domain) again.

confirmed.title: Mixed-signedness symbol comparison in KmpMatcher::step matches values that differ
confirmed.detail: step(const U &c) compares `c == pattern[state]` across types. The evidence (90-prefix_z.md, "mixed-type non-narrowing") and the tester case "mixed-types-no-narrowing" treat this as comparing values. When one side is unsigned and at least as wide as the other, the usual arithmetic conversions turn a signed -1 into UINT_MAX or ULLONG_MAX, so different values compare equal. kmpOccurrences, prefixOccurrences(pattern,text) and the streaming matcher then report false matches, and -Wall gives -Wsign-compare warnings at lines 56 and 57. The tester only checks the unsigned char vs int pair, where promotion to int happens to keep the values. Fix: compare with `std::cmp_equal` when both types are integral and `==` otherwise, through one helper used at lines 56 and 57. Alternatively, document that mixed-signedness symbol types are outside the domain, and add a uint/int regression test either way.

Build with g++ -std=gnu++20 -O2 -Wall -Wextra and you also get -Wsign-compare warnings at lines 56:29 and 57:15.

confirmed.title: prefixOccurrences(pattern, text) needs an iterable text, which contradicts the documented index-only requirement
confirmed.detail: 90-prefix_z.md says: "Constructors require iterable sequences; static prefix/Z functions only require `.size()` and indexing." kmpOccurrences meets this because it indexes text[i]. The sibling overload prefixOccurrences(pattern, text) loops over text with range-for (`for (const auto &c : text)`), so a text type that has only size() and operator[] does not compile. Fix: loop `for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) { matcher.step(text[i]); ... }` with n = int(text.size()), matching kmpOccurrences. Alternatively, change the contract text.

confirmed.title: Public build/encode/add accept ulng codes with no stated domain; double-prime path silently truncates or leaves residues unreduced
confirmed.detail: `encode(ulng x)` returns `{uint(x), uint(x)}` without reducing modulo MOD[i]. `add` assumes both inputs are below MOD and does one subtraction in 32-bit `uint`. `build(int n, F code)` is a public inventory operation and passes `encode(code(i))` straight into `add`. Only the vector<uint> constructor checks the symbol range. Neither the header comment nor 91-stringhash.md (which only says 'callers preserve their invariants') states the allowed range of `code` or of `encode`/`add`/`subtract`/`multiply`, against 03-cpp.md: 'Document in the comment above each struct or free function: domain and width limits'. Codes of 2^32 or more are truncated modulo 2^32 instead of reduced modulo p, which gives deterministic collisions between symbols whose residues differ. Codes in [2^32 - MOD, 2^32) make `a[i] += b[i]` wrap in `uint`. Codes in [MOD[0], 2^32) produce unnormalized residues, so equal residues can compare unequal. Fix: state 'code(i) in [0, MOD[0]) for the double-prime variant, any ulng for WRAP64' in the header comment, and either `assert` that range once per build or reduce with `x % MOD[i]` in `encode`.

Also StringHash<>::add(encode(4000000000), encode(4000000000))[0] prints 2705032697, which is above MOD[0]; the correct residue is 999999951.

This applies to control blocks, function bodies and lambda bodies, and nests: `}}`." Decision log 10-decisions.md:204 also says: "Verified headers that used own-line function closes are normalized during re-audit." This re-audit did not normalize them. Four closes in the header break the rule: line 12 (`isPalindrome` body), line 18 (`maybePalindrome` body), line 27 (the `take` lambda ends with `};` on its own line) and line 30 (`longestPalindrome` body). The fix is to attach each close to the last statement, as in `... : m.even[i] >= len / 2;}`, `return h.get(l, r) == h.reverseGet(l, r);}`, `if (...) { ans = p; }};` and `return ans;}`. This is style only. Behavior is unchanged.
confirmed.repro: rg -n '^\s*\};?$' '/home/Ausp3x/Documents/CompProg Library/07-Strings/08-palindrome_queries.hpp' lists lines 12, 18, 27 and 30.

confirmed.title: Odd and Wheel30 are 3-6x slower than Plain at high endpoints because of branchy per-prime start offsets
confirmed.detail: Every block rescans every base prime with p*p < hi, so at high endpoints the per-prime start computation dominates. Odd adds `if (odd && !(start & 1)) { start += p; }` (lines 44-45), whose branch is mispredicted about half the time; Wheel30 adds `while (!(MASK >> (k % 30) & 1)) { ++k; }` (lines 39-40), which runs 0-5 times unpredictably. Branch-free fix with identical results: for odd p, `lng k = max(p, first / p + (first % p != 0)); if (odd) { k |= 1; } lll start = lll(p) * k;` (p*k is odd iff k is odd), and for Wheel30 a 30-entry next-coprime-residue table `k += NEXT[k % 30];`. Measured on [1e16-1e5, 1e16), block 32768 (reviewer / three skeptics): original Plain 60-82 ms, Odd 189-242 ms, Wheel30 310-418 ms; patched Plain 58-80, Odd 58-76, Wheel30 60-83. On [1e12-2e6, 1e12) original 30/46/72 ms, patched 29/20/23 ms; on [0, 1e8] no regression (patched 531/225/287 vs 534/232/308). 116,640 differential cases (exhaustive l in [-5, 200] with blocks 1, 2, 7, 30, 31 plus 3000 random intervals up to 5e6, all modes) gave 0 mismatches. The evidence 05-Mathematics/95-segmentedsieve.md (lines 25 and 87) wrongly attributes the gap to an expected per-block/base-scan tradeoff; correct it with the code.

confirmed.title: Materialized sieve built from a shared base copies all base primes, contradicting its M bound
confirmed.detail: `bprms = base.bprms;` in the reuse-base constructor, `reset` and `fromClosed(..., base)` copies all pi(sqrt(base.max_value)) primes in time and memory, but nothing reads a prime with p*p >= r (`forEachFactor` stops at line 128, `getPrimeFac(x)` at line 147). The struct comment (lines 91-92) claims `M: O(n + pi(sqrt(R)))` and the setup cost leaves out the copy. Fix: copy only the needed prefix, e.g. `bprms.assign(base.bprms.begin(), upper_bound(base.bprms.begin(), base.bprms.end(), segmented_sieve_detail::root(max(lng(0), r - 1))));`, or, if the full copy is intentional, change the comment to O(n + pi(sqrt(base.max_value))).
confirmed.repro: Build SegmentedSieveBase(1e16-1), then 100 objects SegmentedSieve(100+q, 200+q, base): 510-627 ms total, each storing 5,761,455 primes (46 MB) where 4 are needed; with their own small base the same 100 objects take 0.04 ms.
